assessment.nobel_worthiness: Circuit QED turned a superconducting artificial atom into a controllable, strongly coupled emitter of microwave photons, opening a clean new regime of light-matter interaction (strong coupling, dispersive readout, photon-mediated qubit coupling) and underpinning most present superconducting quantum processors. It is a discovery-level advance in quantum optics, not only an engineering platform, and every physical detail (coupling, dispersive shift, Purcell and decoherence budgets) has been tested extensively. I am close to this field, so I weigh it carefully against the 2025 prize on macroscopic tunnelling in circuits; the two recognise different, complementary steps.
assessment.attribution: Blais, Girvin, Huang, Wallraff and Schoelkopf are the core group: Blais and colleagues made the 2004 theory proposal and Wallraff and Schoelkopf the 2004 Nature experiment. The three credited names are a coherent, fair configuration, but the credited list omits Steven Girvin and Ren-Shou Huang, which I note as a real credit question for the theory side.
assessment.maturity: Strong and fully independent confirmation across many laboratories for over twenty years, and the interpretation is stable. Recognition is timely and arguably mature, with the technology now at the stage where progress is clearly visible.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2025 prize may be seen as too close in the same device family.
Theory-side credit (Girvin, Huang) lies outside the supplied names.
My close involvement in the field could be perceived as a conflict of interest.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The theoretical prediction of the quantum spin Hall effect and Z2 topological insulators, followed by the HgTe edge-transport experiment, opened a new class of quantum matter and a major research direction. The idea is original, clear, and lasting in influence across condensed matter, with a clean connection between a theoretical invariant and measurable edge conductance.
assessment.attribution: Kane and Mele made the decisive theoretical proposal; Molenkamp's group delivered the first experimental realisation in HgTe quantum wells (following Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang, who are not credited here). Hasan led the ARPES identification of 3D topological insulators, which is a separate step. Kane, Mele and Molenkamp is a defensible trio, but the allocation between 2D and 3D parts is unresolved.
assessment.maturity: Predictions are confirmed by multiple independent experiments, and the field is mature and stable. Recognition is timely.
uncertainties: The credited list lacks Bernevig, Zhang and Hughes, who matter for the HgTe prediction.
Hasan's 3D contribution is left out of my trio, and Moore, Balents, Roy and Fu-Kane-Mele are also not on the list.
Compound discovery whose 2D and 3D parts might need different recognition.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Ultracold atoms in optical lattices made many-body Hamiltonians tunable and observable, exemplified by the superfluid to Mott insulator transition, and launched analogue quantum simulation. It is a scientifically deep platform with a long list of demonstrated new regimes, and the work links closely to the quantum simulation goals that I follow in superconducting circuits.
assessment.attribution: Zoller (with Jaksch, Cirac and others) supplied the key theory; Greiner and Bloch carried the decisive experiments. Cirac and Esslinger are also substantial contributors, so the five-name list forces a hard choice of three and a fair prize is not obviously settled. Jaksch is not listed.
assessment.maturity: Confirmed independently by many labs for over twenty years and the interpretation is stable. The recognition is timely, though some of the field has been recognised through related prizes (BEC, 2001; Hall and Hansch, 2005).
uncertainties: The choice of three from five credited names is contestable.
Overlap with earlier cold-atom Nobel prizes could weigh against it.
Practical quantum advantage from analogue simulators is still unsettled, though that does not bear on the discovery itself.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Predicting flat bands at the magic angle in twisted bilayer graphene and observing correlated insulators and superconductivity in them opened moire quantum materials, a genuinely new regime of controllable strongly correlated physics. The impact on condensed matter is substantial and growing.
assessment.attribution: Bistritzer and MacDonald made the 2011 flat-band prediction and Jarillo-Herrero's group made the 2018 experimental discovery of correlated states and superconductivity. Eva Andrei's group had earlier observations of flat bands; whether she merits a share is a real allocation question, and the three-person limit forces a choice.
assessment.maturity: Reproduced by many groups, but the origin of the superconductivity is still debated, so the interpretation is not fully settled. Recognition is early but the central results are robust.
uncertainties: The pairing mechanism of the superconductivity is unresolved.
Credit competition with Andrei and with the earlier theory of Lopes dos Santos, Peres and Castro Neto.
Possible prematurity compared with older candidates.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The observation of quantized conductance in ballistic point contacts in 1988 made visible the basic fact of one-dimensional ballistic transport and gave a clean textbook demonstration of Landauer-type conductance quantization. It founded modern mesoscopic transport and the quantum point contacts used in later qubit and interferometer devices. It is a compact, clear and lasting experiment, the kind that I value, though its conceptual novelty relative to Landauer's picture is somewhat modest.
assessment.attribution: The 1988 papers by van Wees et al. (Delft) and Wharam et al. (Cambridge) were simultaneous and independent, with Pepper's group central to the Cambridge side and the gate technology. The trio is a natural configuration, though the detailed credit within each large collaboration is not something I have verified.
assessment.maturity: Reproduced in innumerable devices over decades; fully mature. The delay may suggest that the committee has not found it prize-sized, which is a concern.
uncertainties: Whether the committee sees it as a discovery of a new regime or a confirmation of Landauer theory.
The long time since 1988 means the case may have been passed over repeatedly.
Contributions of others in the Delft and Cambridge groups (e.g. Beenakker, van Houten, Williamson) are outside the credited list.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The Rydberg blockade combined with optical tweezer arrays gives programmable, strongly interacting neutral-atom arrays for quantum simulation and gate operations, with demonstrations of large coherent many-body systems. It is a rapidly maturing quantum platform with significant physics results (quantum phases, spin liquids, high-fidelity gates).
assessment.attribution: Zoller and Lukin formulated key proposals (Jaksch et al., Lukin et al. 2001) and Lukin and Browaeys, along with Saffman, led the experimental development. Saffman's contribution to blockade gates is also substantial, so excluding him is a real choice. Many other groups (Bernien, Endres, Weiss) are not credited.
assessment.maturity: Confirmed by several independent groups, but the field is still evolving quickly, and fault-tolerant demonstrations are recent. I consider it somewhat early relative to its likely long-term significance.
uncertainties: Premature relative to the pace of continuing progress.
Attribution is spread among theorists, experimentalists and tweezer-array pioneers beyond the three credited.
Prize overlap with other cold-atom awards.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Cavity optomechanics established radiation-pressure coupling of light to mechanical motion and enabled ground-state cooling and quantum control of macroscopic mechanical oscillators, with squeezing and entanglement. It is solid quantum optics that connects naturally with my own work on microwave circuits coupled to mechanics and phonons.
assessment.attribution: Kippenberg, Aspelmeyer and Painter were all central in the experimental demonstrations of sideband cooling and quantum-regime control, while the credited list omits Vahala, Harris, Lehnert and Cleland, who made decisive contributions to cooling and quantum-ground-state demonstrations. A fair three-way configuration is difficult.
assessment.maturity: Reproduced across many platforms and the interpretation is firm, though no single decisive result stands out as the discovery, which makes it hard to identify the prize-defining moment.
uncertainties: No single prize-defining discovery and a diffuse credit landscape.
Key contributors in electromechanics (Lehnert, Cleland) fall outside the credited names.
Applications remain mostly in sensing rather than a separate new regime.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Quantum key distribution applies quantum measurement and entanglement to secure communication, with BB84 and the Ekert protocol as lasting conceptual contributions that connect foundations and technology. It is original and clear, and has produced a large experimental field.
assessment.attribution: Bennett and Brassard introduced BB84, and Ekert proposed the entanglement-based protocol; Jian-Wei Pan led long-distance and satellite demonstrations. Which of the protocol conceptual and experimental pieces should be rewarded is unresolved, and the three theorists would exclude the experimental line.
assessment.maturity: Protocols are well confirmed, but the practical security and long-distance deployments are still developing. Prior prize recognition of entanglement (2022) overlaps in part.
uncertainties: The 2022 prize on entangled photons covers close ground.
Distinction between conceptual protocol invention and experimental realisation within a single prize.
Practical security under real devices is not fully established.
